rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to capture all 10 compounds and identify crowded retention regions. Moderate temperature and gradient duration provide a useful baseline for optimizing separation and run time.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin is retained. Keeping temperature and solvent endpoints fixed isolates the effect of gradient steepness.
Test temperature-driven selectivity changes to separate the crowded middle peaks without lengthening the gradient. Higher temperature may also shorten retention, preserving the zero time penalty.

Test an intermediate temperature to balance the middle-peak crowding at 40 °C against the near-coelution seen at 60 °C. Retain the fast gradient, which has produced no time penalty at either temperature.

A slightly shallower gradient may resolve the near-coeluting middle pair at 60 °C while retaining the improved separation elsewhere. The last peak should still elute early enough to avoid a time penalty.

Test 55 °C to balance the two temperature-sensitive middle separations, using a slightly shallower gradient to improve resolution. The last peak is expected before 8 minutes, preserving the zero time penalty.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to seek more resolution margin while retaining the temperature balance that achieved CRF 1.000. The last peak is expected near 8 minutes, potentially preserving the zero time penalty.

Increase the starting organic fraction to test whether a shorter separation can retain the maximum CRF already achieved. This also probes how the two marginal middle-pair resolutions respond to a change in gradient starting conditions.

Slightly flatten the gradient to improve the R = 1.29 middle-pair separation while retaining the higher starting organic fraction. This may recover CRF 1.000 with the last peak still before 8 minutes.

Further flatten the gradient to bring the marginal R = 1.47 separation above 1.5 while potentially retaining zero time penalty. This tests for another maximum-score method with more balanced resolution margins.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to seek larger middle-pair resolution margins while keeping the last peak below 8 minutes. The maximum CRF is already established; this tests an alternative method with potentially better separation margins.

With the maximum CRF already secured, explore the untested low-temperature selectivity regime for another fully resolved, fast method. Keeping the scouting gradient endpoints and 10-minute duration isolates the temperature effect.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction moves the temperature-sensitive middle pair away from its near-coelution at 60 °C. This explores a faster alternative while the maximum-score method from injection 6 remains established.

Test a steeper gradient to shift the remaining close middle pair farther past its selectivity crossover at 60 °C. This could improve its resolution while shortening the separation, although neighboring pairs may lose resolution.

Increase the starting organic fraction to test whether the remaining close middle pair separates further at 60 °C. Returning to a 10-minute gradient should help preserve neighboring separations, while the early pair will need monitoring for compression.

Preserve injection 6’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while shortening the programmed ramp. Since all peaks previously eluted before 10 minutes, this should reproduce its maximum CRF with a lower final organic fraction.

Test a gradient slope between those of injections 9 and 10, targeting resolution above 1.5 for both limiting pairs with the last peak before 8 minutes. This may retain CRF 1.000 with a better balance of resolution and time margins.

Preserve injection 10’s gradient slope and temperature while lowering the endpoint and shortening the programmed ramp. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, potentially retaining CRF 1.000 and its resolution margins.

Probe the temperature sensitivity of injection 17’s maximum-score method by lowering temperature one grid step. This will test whether its balanced middle-pair separations persist at a neighboring temperature.

Complete the neighboring-temperature test around injection 17’s maximum-score method. This will characterize the upper-temperature selectivity limit and determine whether full resolution persists at 60 °C.

Retain injection 6’s successful gradient slope and temperature while reducing the endpoint to 0.65 and the ramp to 8 minutes. The last peak should still elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, preserving the maximum CRF.

Keep the successful gradient slope but begin the final hold earlier, testing whether a lower endpoint still permits maximum CRF. The first nine peaks should be unchanged; the main question is whether the last peak remains within the zero-penalty time window.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 10 to improve the close middle separation while retaining the favorable 55 °C selectivity. The last peak is expected near 8.2 minutes, where injection 22 indicates a zero time penalty remains possible.

Use a slope close to injection 23’s maximum-score method with a lower endpoint and shorter programmed ramp. The observed trends predict both limiting resolutions above 1.5 and the last peak near 8.3 minutes, preserving zero time penalty.

Use the final injection to test whether the successful 55 °C selectivity permits a shorter gradient while retaining full resolution. The maximum CRF is already secured; this probes a faster alternative to injection 6.
